utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone. Doctor, do you hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can hear you very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Good morning to you, Doctor.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We are hearing the French translation. Okay, let's continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I should like to go quickly over some matters that I believe can be answered with a yes or no, to make things more efficient. First of all, do you know that I issued a great number of orders concerning the protection of civilians, the observation of International Humanitarian Law, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: YOUSSEF HAJIR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell me, what was the population of Dobrinja?

utterances.speaker: YOUSSEF HAJIR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before the war, around 40.000. During the war, I believe it was around 25.000. Nobody can give you a precise answer to that, but these are approximate figures.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you go to attend meetings of the Command of the 155th Brigade?

utterances.speaker: YOUSSEF HAJIR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Never. They never asked me, and I never went, nor was I part of the command, finally.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: How about your deputy? He was commander of the Medical Service. What was the name of that doctor, the deputy director?

utterances.speaker: YOUSSEF HAJIR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dr. Zlatko Kravic. First it was Dr. Radoncic, and then Zlatko Kravic as chief of the Medical Section of the brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Was he invited to meetings of the command?

utterances.speaker: YOUSSEF HAJIR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Honestly, I never asked him, and he never told me that he went to such meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let me summarise, then. You did not receive regular daily combat reports?

utterances.speaker: YOUSSEF HAJIR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And you were not involved in the planning of operations, nor in their later analysis?

utterances.speaker: YOUSSEF HAJIR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not a soldier, really, nor would I know how to analyse military operations, nor would I know how to plan them. That's not my job. I never wanted to interfere with jobs I know nothing about.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Were you informed, officially or in any other way, of developments in the theatre of war?

utterances.speaker: YOUSSEF HAJIR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sometimes somebody would drop by and tell us what's going on, but nothing official.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you now take your amalgamated statement. I'll try to go quickly over certain paragraphs. In your book, you said you had 1200 or so surgeries and around 6.000 minor surgeries in the out-patient clinic, including 1.000-plus peacetime injuries and around 5.000 wartime injuries. That is approximately 6200 surgeries in total. Now, why do larger numbers appear in your statement; 5.000 major surgeries and 16.000 patients in total?

utterances.speaker: YOUSSEF HAJIR [Resumed]
utterances.text: You see, about exact numbers of injuries and surgeries, I don't know those exact numbers, and nobody will ever know, because no precise records were kept. We never wanted to waste time on that. I don't know what happened to four or five protocols that went missing and we never could trace, whether somebody stole them or whatever happened. All I had was what I had to hand. As for the lost protocols, we tried to track them down. We involved the police as well, but we never found them. That's the reason for this confusion about numbers.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In fact, it appeared to me that in a population of 30.000, 16.000 would have gone through your clinic. Yesterday, you mentioned that there were some people who passed through the tunnel and got injured there. Was the frequency of passages through the tunnel so high that you could get so many patients out of these people?

utterances.speaker: YOUSSEF HAJIR [Resumed]
utterances.text: The tunnel was 120, 130 centimetres high and it was 800 metres long. You could not stand up properly. You would hit iron beams. It was simply that you had to go through that tunnel for such a long time, maintaining a completely unnatural posture. You can imagine how many people passed in both directions. Injuries were frequent.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: How many people went through?

utterances.speaker: YOUSSEF HAJIR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, people went through to get to the other side to visit their families, or to get groceries, to find food, to give their children -- there are so many reasons why people went to the tunnel. Nobody would do it just like that, because it was dangerous. You never knew when you would be hit by a shell while entering or leaving. Nobody went there on a whim or for enjoyment. It was because of dire need.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did entire units of the 1st Corps leave the city and come back through that tunnel?

utterances.speaker: YOUSSEF HAJIR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Honestly, I personally never saw anything like that. It's possible, but I've never seen it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Where would they assemble if they had to go through the tunnel? What would be the assembly point? Because they couldn't go all together. They would have to go one by one; right?

utterances.speaker: YOUSSEF HAJIR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So first of all they would have to gather somewhere close to the entrance to the tunnel?

utterances.speaker: YOUSSEF HAJIR [Resumed]
utterances.text: If what you're saying is true, then that would be right. They couldn't go in all at once.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now see 1D2686. I hope you will see it in your e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Have you ever heard of Nedzad Ajnadzic [Realtime transcript read in error "Inadzic"]?

utterances.speaker: YOUSSEF HAJIR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe Nenad Ajnadzic was commander of the 1st Corps. I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: That's right. Could we now take a look at our electronic mail. I believe we are now going to get this exhibit. The record should be corrected. The name should be spelled as A-J-nadzic, instead of I. Could you now take a look at this text, where it says the tunnel was dug out and its purpose was to provide a safe way for providing logistical support to units in Sarajevo, but also a connection with the free territory of the BH. That's the paragraph after the enumeration of these systems.

utterances.speaker: YOUSSEF HAJIR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't see it. It doesn't matter. In any case, it's possible. Yes, the purpose of the tunnel was to make things easier, to make it easier to get in and out, not only for civilians, but for soldiers, when necessary.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we see the next page, please. Sorry, that's a different document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: On this page, we see there were D and B structures connecting Dobrinja and Butmir, passing through -- below the runway of the Sarajevo Airport?

utterances.speaker: YOUSSEF HAJIR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The task was entrusted to the BH Army, the 1st Corps, and in the beginning of 1993, in the greatest secrecy, they started digging the tunnel?

utterances.speaker: YOUSSEF HAJIR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can I comment?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: YOUSSEF HAJIR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before digging the tunnel, you see, you cannot hermetically close in 300.000 people in an area. If you had left the corridor open, you, maybe half of the people would have left, because everybody had needs. They had children to feed, they had families. Before the tunnel was dug out, people simply ran across the runway. Many people were hurt by sniper fire from the Serbian side, and if not from the Serbian side, then by the French Battalion that was responsible for that runway. What do you expect, if you close a person in their own home without letting them walk, breathe? Really, Colleague Karadzic, it's not realistic to expect that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have this page admitted so I can call another one?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What page is it, Mr. Karadzic; 257?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, and that's Exhibit 1D2686, marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I take it there's no objection from the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: No objection to it being marked for identification, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, that will be marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As MFI D856, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we get 1D2687.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know, Dr. Hajir, that the Serbian side had offered corridors for civilian traffic and commercial traffic, on the condition that no military assets or forces be allowed to use these corridors?

utterances.speaker: YOUSSEF HAJIR [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the first I hear of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I'm afraid they kept many things from you, or perhaps you were too busy and were unable to find out.

utterances.speaker: YOUSSEF HAJIR [Resumed]
utterances.text: That may well be, but somebody would have spoken up. You see, people were coming and going all the time. People were passing through hospital in great numbers. Somebody would have said something. I never heard of anything like that, really.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you take a look at this page 259, where it says: "In the night, when the tunnel was completed, 600 soldiers, under full equipment, passed through it immediately, and they went directly to Mount Igman to stop the aggressor's offensive. At the same time in the same night, around five tons of military materiel and equipment was delivered to Sarajevo the same way."

utterances.speaker: YOUSSEF HAJIR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't see it, but what's your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is it consistent with what you said a moment ago, that the through-put of this tunnel was very high, both for soldiers and civilians?

utterances.speaker: YOUSSEF HAJIR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very possible.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have this admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It will be admitted in the same number, and we'll mark it for identification. It's a part of the same book, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but it's just a different page, 259. Also, 258 and 259 we can admit. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 8 of your statement, you say that Dobrinja, in the beginning, was not completely surrounded, and do you agree that, in view of the tunnel, it was never completely encircled, just like Sarajevo wasn't, because the traffic through the tunnel was quite substantial?

utterances.speaker: YOUSSEF HAJIR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mentioned the time when the war began. With the opening of the tunnel, it was a little bit, but, you know, the capacity of the tunnel and the possibility of allowing the traffic through was quite limited.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I wanted to ask you: For some of your assertions -- for all of your assertions, do you have proof or are these your impressions? Very often, you, yourself, say that, It is my impression. For example, in paragraph 14, the last sentence states that it was your impression that the Serbs only wanted to kill, and that is one of the reasons they did not take Dobrinja. Were they able to kill you easily at the check-point at Vraca?

utterances.speaker: YOUSSEF HAJIR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they could have. But then how to explain the sealing off of the town, the hermetical closing off of the town, especially Dobrinja? Dobrinja was a residential area. There were no factories, there was nothing there. How can you fire? And you know that there are children there, the elderly, women, who are defenceless. I had a child, seven or eight years old, shot by a sniper directly in the heart. I mean, the sniper could have seen that this was a child. I am speaking openly, Colleague. These are facts that were happening that I could observe around me, so these are not my impressions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right. But do you know that the other side, the side of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, or, actually, more the police, was also active in sniper killings of Serbs and Muslims?

utterances.speaker: YOUSSEF HAJIR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that there was several attempts to attack Nedzarici, not for the purpose of occupation, but for the purpose of clearing those sniper nests. This is from what I understood, as far as a number of these actions that were not successful because of poor co-ordination. You say, Organise this, Organise that. These few brigades that were on the line were unable to co-ordinate and carry this out and to secure a safer passage through Mojmilo or other parts of town.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that Nedzarici was a purely Serbian neighbourhood, with private homes that were mostly -- that mostly had a ground floor and first floor?

utterances.speaker: YOUSSEF HAJIR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The majority, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that this settlement was inferior in relation to Vojnicko Polje, Alipasino Polje, where they had high-rise buildings of some 10, 15 storeys?

utterances.speaker: YOUSSEF HAJIR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely, yes, but that is proof that they did not want Nedzarici, because they could have. It seems to me these two or three brigades that were around could have taken Nedzarici. They just wanted to get rid of the sniper nests that were constantly firing at people. Well, at least, this is what I know. I'm telling you what I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You agree, probably, that the Serbs could probably have captured Dobrinja, but they didn't do that because there would have been many civilian casualties; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: YOUSSEF HAJIR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, with the military force that they had and three military barracks, they could have easily taken it in the beginning, and there wouldn't have been that many civilian casualties then.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm concerned with this first sentence from paragraph 14, that: "The Serbs were absolutely targeting civilians." Is this an impression or are you able to give us some kind of evidence for this assertion?

utterances.speaker: YOUSSEF HAJIR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yesterday, you showed a paper where you could see injured people. They were all fighters. You didn't show all the papers that you had that would show that there were tenfold more civilians. What can I say? When you tried to save lives, for the most part, people are coming -- actually, very few soldiers came, compared to the number of civilians that came. And I'm telling you, because I know, I was there, I could see what was happening. What would be my impression if the situation that I had was like that?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And the next sentence says that: "There were no military units there in the beginning, and there was no organised army." Is this the reason why you concluded that civilians were harmed, rather than soldiers?

utterances.speaker: YOUSSEF HAJIR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely, Mr. Karadzic. I am telling you, definitely, there were none. Like you said, there was the Patriotic League, the 110th, the 140th. Believe me, I would have seen that, people would have told me. There was nothing like that in Dobrinja. These were young men, 20 years old, that would come, who were changing clothes and taking pistols and rifles. They didn't have any heavy weapons. This is the kind of thing I saw in Dobrinja. I'm not saying that there weren't heavier weapons in other places, but there were some lighter weapons that were used among protesters. There was multi-barrelled weapons. Perhaps I saw a tank -- I never saw a tank on this side. So this is mostly what I saw.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters note we are having difficulty understanding the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I understand that you were busy, you were unable to see that. Do you know how many fighters of the 155th Brigade, which existed before August 1992 under a different name, how many fighters of the 155th Brigade were wounded?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before you answer, Dr. Hajir: Yes, Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Perhaps the witness's microphone needs to be turned up, because the interpreters are having trouble understanding the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, I was just about to pay attention to that. Could you, Dr. Hajir, speak to the microphone. Yes. A bit closer, yes. And please put a pause between your answer -- between the question and your answer, kindly. Yes. Could you answer the question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that I already answered. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I'm afraid they didn't hear you. So it's not in dispute that the brigade existed. Yesterday, we showed a document that in August, as already finished, completed brigade, it became part of the 1st Corps, and Muslim information indicates that the brigade had 5.000 fighters. How many of these men or fighters in that brigade were killed and how many were wounded?

utterances.speaker: YOUSSEF HAJIR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really couldn't tell you that. I really don't know. We never did any kind of statistical calculations. You can see that all the statistical data, the numbers are problematic, and there was much more, in terms of numbers, than what is stated in books.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In the case of General Perisic, on the 29th of January, 2009, on page 2998, you said that you didn't differentiate between civilian and military casualties or patients; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: YOUSSEF HAJIR [Resumed]
utterances.text: We never differentiated between people. People were there, and they needed help if they were hurt, so we didn't make any distinctions. If you make a difference on one side, then there will be a difference made on the other side. One needs to treat everybody equally on all sides. And I think that, in that sense, I acted properly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right, thank you. I agree with you. It's a fact that many fought in civilian clothing, as you, yourself, confirmed yesterday. Can you please tell me, these 5.000 soldiers, how did they move around in Dobrinja? There were four large battalions and there were two others, one engineering one and another one, I don't what kind it was. How did they move around and manoeuvre around Dobrinja, in such a small area? They must have been very visible and something that would grab the attention of the Serbian Army.

utterances.speaker: YOUSSEF HAJIR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never saw any gathering, moving around, and walking in Dobrinja. I don't know of any barracks belonging to the Bosnian Army, either. Things like that weren't there. They didn't gather at the command, either. There were about one or two men at the command who were guarding the commander, guards. As for the rest, I really don't know where they were. Probably, everybody was at home, mostly. Those who were coming from town later, I don't know where they were billeted. I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: If they were at their homes, does that mean that that was their combat deployment or disposition, to be in their buildings?

utterances.speaker: YOUSSEF HAJIR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, where would the people go? They couldn't walk around, they couldn't go home. I mean, it doesn't mean that it was their wartime disposition or assignment to stay at home.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I look at 1D1100 now, please, so that you can see what that looked like on the 23rd of May, 1992, precisely what you were saying, where all the fighters were assembled in Dobrinja.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Were there any trenches or any roads that they could have used otherwise? I mean, this is a major --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I'm sorry for interrupting, Your Honour, but can Mr. Karadzic direct me to the exhibit which says there was 5.000 Muslims in the 155th Mountain Brigade, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The Chamber was discussing that. But, Doctor, Mr. Karadzic put several questions to you on the basis that there were 5.000 Muslim fighters in the region. Can you confirm that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Absolutely not. I really don't know. I mean, if you count the auxiliary services, logistics, and drivers, and whatnot, I still think that you wouldn't get 5.000. I don't think so. Anyway, like I said, we never counted, nobody ever told me anything like that, so I don't know the exact number. But I'm saying that this number of 5.000 cannot be. It's too high a number for that area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Can you give us a rough idea how many soldiers there would be, roughly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Whatever I were to tell you, it wouldn't be the truth. It wouldn't even be close to the truth. I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We agree that there were four battalions. Do you agree that a battalion numbers between four to six companies?

utterances.speaker: YOUSSEF HAJIR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, I really don't know how many companies a battalion should have. I really don't know. I'm not avoiding an answer. I'm just telling you what I know. And what I know, I will gladly tell you. What I don't know, I don't know. I thought that yesterday we had put a full stop to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You confirmed yesterday, did you not, that there were four battalions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He mentioned six battalions. What I know, I think that there were four battalions. I don't know if there were more. I never heard of that. I wasn't from where those battalions were, and I don't know where they were, you know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree, Dr. Hajir, that there was a command of the 155th Brigade there with the HQ units, the commands of four battalions with their staff units, and the commands of 15 to 17 companies with their staff units?

utterances.speaker: YOUSSEF HAJIR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Where? Are you thinking of Dobrinja?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: That's the 155th. It was deployed?

utterances.speaker: YOUSSEF HAJIR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, that's correct, it did exist.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we now look at this document. We do have a translation. This is an intelligence report of the 23rd of May, which states that: "Just in the Zikice Jovanovica Spanca Street at numbers," and it gives the odd numbers here, also the even numbers - there are some 20 numbers, "that there were strong concentrations of Green Berets. On each floor, there were two members of the Green Berets in order to prevent the movement and communication between the residents." And so on and so forth: "About 40 per cent of the Serbian population moved out of those buildings." And so on. These are armed with automatic rifles, machine-guns, snipers, hand-grenades, and they are being supplied with food every day. Did they conceal so many things from you that you didn't know this?

utterances.speaker: YOUSSEF HAJIR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am telling you -- I don't know how to convince you. This is absolutely unknown to me. Perhaps I would have known more had I asked. I really never wanted to ask where they were, who they were, what they were doing. I was doing my job, the task that I set myself, and I did that properly. As for how others were doing their job and what they did, please don't ask me about that, because I know very, very little of things that were going on around me.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I understand that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Again, I'm sorry for interrupting. It was my understanding that Mr. Karadzic called up 1D01101. Is that the document we're supposed to be looking at, because I don't see the information contained therein that he's been stating.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: No first was 1100, and next will be 1101.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have this document admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, if I may, 1D1100 has been admitted as Exhibit D330.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I didn't know it's admitted. Can we now see 1D1101. And also information as to its status; is it already an exhibit? There it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Dr. Hajir, can you look at it? It's another intelligence report of the 23rd of May. It says the Green Berets are stationed in the elementary school Petar Dokic in Cengic Vila. And about Dobrinja, it says: "We also received intelligence that Osman Lunja and a certain Prutinja harassed 29 Serbs from the Remzije Pehlimanovica Street. A certain Serif, known as Kise, from Dobrinja, imprisoned 10 individuals, 10 Serbs, and was aided by a certain Haris ...," and they tortured the prisoners as well: "On that occasion, they singled out Milorad Djurdjevic just because he was originally from Foca. They forced the prisoners to admit they had been snipers, and they also inquired as to where prominent Serbs were located." Did you hear of this man Kise? He was notorious in Dobrinja.

utterances.speaker: YOUSSEF HAJIR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know this Kise, but I know nothing about this incident. This Kise man is a braggart, arrogant, full of himself. He came by a few times.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we have this admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I don't see a basis to admit this, Mr. Karadzic. The doctor knows Kise, but nothing else. I don't see the point of putting this to the doctor.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right, I understand. The doctor, himself, said he didn't know about these things going on, so we can try it with someone else. Thank you, Dr. Hajir. We'll move on through your statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you help us remember how many of these incidents there were involving several or more casualties? We know about one football-match, and we know about the line of people queuing for humanitarian aid. How many incidents were there where civilians were hurt in larger numbers, let's say more than three or more than five?

utterances.speaker: YOUSSEF HAJIR [Resumed]
utterances.text: You can see it in my book. As far as information reached me, I describe very honestly every incident and how many people were hurt. Whether seven or eight people were hurt in each one of them, I don't really know, but it was really deliberate. People were targeted while waiting for water, while queuing for humanitarian aid. Doesn't that tell you anything? It's not only military targets; it was civilian targets, no matter how wretched and miserable these people were, and you never took the trouble to condemn such actions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I'm afraid you're not very well informed. I did condemn them, and I asked for investigations. And we'll demonstrate, concerning a few incidents, exactly who fired. But since you mentioned that a thousand civilians were killed in Dobrinja, we have to identify in which incidents this happened, how this happened. These had to be dramatic events if a thousand civilians were killed over 1200 days, whereas there were whole months passing without a single person killed. So apart from the football-match and the queue for humanitarian aid, which feature in my indictment, are there any more incidents involving massive casualties that we can identify?

utterances.speaker: YOUSSEF HAJIR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, every day injured people came to the hospital. After two or three years, we still don't have complete statistics, but there was not a single day passing without at least 10 or 15 injured people coming to be treated. I don't know what kind of military or non-military events they got hurt in. These statistics are not reliable. I'm just telling you that nobody really was concerned with numbers at that time. I told you what our priorities were, to what extent we had our hands full. One of these massacres, remember from my book, this woman, Dr. Krlic, came to help out, and she found her son dead. He got killed while helping an elderly woman carry water. How would you react if that happened in the Serbian part of Sarajevo, in a Serbian area?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I agree with you. Every death is a tragic event for that person and for his or her family. But we have to deal with statistics here, which you say are not reliable, so we have to take this number of 1.000 dead civilians as a very relative number?

utterances.speaker: YOUSSEF HAJIR [Resumed]
utterances.text: It could be even more.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Where would they be buried?

utterances.speaker: YOUSSEF HAJIR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, the parks were full of graves. There was one graveyard in Dobrinja 3 that was so packed there was not an inch of land to dig anymore. People buried bodies outside their homes, in their yards, in their gardens. It's tragic when you pass through the street, any street, and see all the places where people are buried.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We saw on that footage yesterday several graves along the road. A thousand graves would be something like the Arlington Cemetery. Why don't we see, in any movies, in any newspapers, a photograph like that, showing at least 100, if not 1.000, graves? How come there are no pictures showing large graveyards full of civilian graves?

utterances.speaker: YOUSSEF HAJIR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now, how would I know that? I did not take any pictures. I never even went out to look. But the number of dead is large. Some people were just driving their dead away somewhere in the city. Some families came belatedly to pick up the bodies and bury them. If you're talking about pictures, there is a place close to C-4, close to the occupied airport settlement, where there was a large cemetery, for instance. Maybe Serbs took more pictures than we did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The Serbs would take that the airport neighbourhood was liberated, whereas you say it was occupied?

utterances.speaker: YOUSSEF HAJIR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm talking about C-4, which is close, next to the airport neighbourhood. C-4, if you know where that is, comes before the airport neighbourhood and then follows C-5. On one side, there is the Nedzarici village, and on the other side, there are multi-storey buildings.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that we should take into account and acknowledge the statistics kept by the BH Army, both in terms of the numbers of the 155th Brigade and in terms of the number of "sahids"? That's what they called martyrs, that's what they call their dead who got killed in the fighting, as opposed to civilians?

utterances.speaker: YOUSSEF HAJIR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, if you use the term properly, but that term was also used for civilians. We were forced to be there by violent means. We were being shot at. And although in terms of religion, they cannot be really considered as "sahids," martyrs, but they were still considered as such.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But if the families received certificates of privatizations and awards, and if they were granted amounts normally allocated to "sahid" families, can we then take it that these people were fighters, rather than civilians, because civilian families got smaller amounts?

utterances.speaker: YOUSSEF HAJIR [Resumed]
utterances.text: You keep talking about rewards. Take me, for instance, the kind of work that I did for all the people there, and you know what I got in return? They closed my hospital. And they did give me the 6th of April decoration, that's true. The Serbs gave it to me, but nothing more. I just went back to the clinical centre to a position lower than I occupied before. What kind of reward did I get? I'm just asking you because you keep talking about these rewards. I, for instance, wasn't part of the SDA. I wasn't part of any party. Maybe that's the reason, maybe that's the general approach. I wouldn't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Dr. Hajir, I believe your contribution is priceless, from a humanitarian point of view, but I'm trying to establish here how many dead were civilians and how many dead were soldiers. Do you know that the state provided tombstones free of charge for "sahids," which they didn't do for civilians?

utterances.speaker: YOUSSEF HAJIR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that that was the case in Kovaci and in some other places, they provided tombstones for people who got killed in the fighting.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know that the BH Army commissioned 40.000 aiming devices for "sahids," and 39.000 were actually delivered?

utterances.speaker: YOUSSEF HAJIR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know that, really.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You mentioned Zelimir Vidovic. I'm really sorry about him. He was my football player. I was in Sarajevo when he played. But have you heard about Josip Bukal? He played for the Zeleznice Team.

utterances.speaker: YOUSSEF HAJIR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we were friends. He came to see me more than once.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know that Josip Bukal, who, by the way, is a Croat, rescued a large number of Serbs from Dobrinja, and these people owe him their lives and are very grateful to him?

utterances.speaker: YOUSSEF HAJIR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really didn't hear about that. But all of us would save people when we could, and I did when I could. I never refused anyone. I never failed to do whatever I could for people. I believe that Bukal would do the same, but I really, to tell the truth, didn't see that Serbs were in danger. There was a discussion we had with the Serbs who were on the staff. We were talking amongst us, and there were some people who were unhappy about some incidents and quarrels internally, but it was all on the verbal level. Take this Djurdjica Juric, who worked with us. Her daughter was shot by a sniper from your side. She came there, and I offered her an apartment close to the hospital so that she can be nearby. She refused because she lived in another flat with her family. Her father-in-law was killed outside his home. That's next to that school which is half Serbian, half Muslim. I don't know the name of the school. They lived very close by, in an apartment building. Bukal is a great humanist, and I believe, easily, that he helped whenever he could. I really didn't see that Serbs were in any danger. If I had seen anything like it, I would have done all in my power to help them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I don't doubt that for a minute. And if you had been commander of Dobrinja, it would have been much better. But you say, in paragraph 42 of your statement, that there were 120 and more injured at the football-match. 130 to 140 persons injured.

utterances.speaker: YOUSSEF HAJIR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, probably more than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But in the Galic case, on page 1716, lines 17 to 24, you said there were 35 soldiers injured and 55 civilians, and that 6 soldiers and 5 civilians got killed.

utterances.speaker: YOUSSEF HAJIR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I really don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you remember reprimanding or asking the commander of the 155th Brigade why he had organised that football-match close to the front-line?

utterances.speaker: YOUSSEF HAJIR [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a huge folly, and I told him so the same day. But he said they wanted it. What could I do? I said, You were the commander, you should have stopped it. There is just a line of buildings separating that football pitch from the front-line, from the Serbian lines. He should have been replaced, in fact, just before that, but he was, instead, appointed commander -- re-appointed commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In paragraphs 48 to 51 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a moment. Yes, Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I'm sorry. The proposition that Mr. Karadzic just put to the witness that he said in the Galic case on page 1716 that 35 soldiers were injured and -- 35 soldiers were injured and 55 civilians, and that 6 soldiers and 5 civilians got killed, that's actually Ms. Filipovic reading out a document, and I can't quite now work out which document it is, but it wasn't the witness's answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: In any event, the witness said he didn't know. Let's move on, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In paragraphs 48 through 51, you speak about problems with water. Did you know that the government of the federation, that is, the Sarajevo Muslim Croat government, created, deliberately, huge disruptions in water supply?

utterances.speaker: YOUSSEF HAJIR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know that. In fact, I don't know. But how would they be able to do that? Why would they do that? Leaving people without water is the same as killing them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you know that water supply depends on electricity supply, and whenever the transformer station in Bacevo is hit, the water supply stops?

utterances.speaker: YOUSSEF HAJIR [Resumed]
utterances.text: You know, I never gave any thought to the routes of water supply.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you know that we never closed the water from Jahorina, from Bistrica, but we actually shared with Sarajevo, a little bit for Pale and a little bit for Sarajevo, and the only water restrictions came from Bacevo, from the Bosna River source, because of electricity cuts?

utterances.speaker: YOUSSEF HAJIR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know that. Well, you can put yourself in my place. You know, what would you think? There was constantly a shortage of water, but we had water supplies. Mr. Dusko, who is a very good friend of mine - he's deceased now - he obtained a 25.000-litre water cistern for the needs of the hospital. We brought that to the shopping centre, and we connected it to the water supply. So when the water was cut off, we would have water. In the beginning, we would bring it in buckets from the well. Later, we resolved it in this way. And what you are saying, I really don't know. I would have liked -- I really would have liked -- I even listened to "SRNA" regularly. Thousands of things that happened in front of your very eyes, they would turn 180 degrees around. Serbs, who were leaving in order to be accepted wherever they were going, were labelling and saying things because of political interest. Mr. Karadzic, you have to differentiate between what is true and what isn't. There is a significant difference. I mean, there was a case that happened in front of my eyes, and then in "SRNA" that event would be presented 180 degrees differently and it would be against the Muslims. That's why I stopped listening.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know that these 300.000 -- 350.000 citizens from paragraph 50 included 50.000 to 70.000 Serbs?

utterances.speaker: YOUSSEF HAJIR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that there was a large number of them, but I don't know how many.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And do you believe that we would have abused those 50.000 to 70.000 Serbs only to harm the rest of the population that was Muslim and Croat? Would we have done something like that deliberately?

utterances.speaker: YOUSSEF HAJIR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Practice indicates that you did. You were shooting. Do you know how many Serbs were killed from these shells? I mean, my heart really pains when I think of all the large number of Serbs and their families that were casualties because of this, not just Muslim families. And I'm saying this because I know. These were wonderful people who were full of goodness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And here, in paragraph 56, you talk about the suicide rate. Is it correct that during your stay there, there were five to six suicides?

utterances.speaker: YOUSSEF HAJIR [Resumed]
utterances.text: There weren't more than that, at least not to my knowledge and what was reported to the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know that, annually, the average rate of suicide is 15 applied to 100.000 citizens in Serbia? In Slovenia, this rate is 27, and for Vojvodina, 2, and for Hungary and Finland, it's 28?

utterances.speaker: YOUSSEF HAJIR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, this figure is quite small. I spoke in -- I was surprised, myself. I mean, there wasn't a significant suicide rate. I'm also surprised. I think that the rate of suicides now is much higher than it was during the war. I'm talking about Dobrinja, at least.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right, thank you. In paragraph 59, it happened that you say that the Serbs were preventing civilians from leaving Sarajevo. Do you know that Serbs always asked for free passage of civilians, and that the Muslim side did not allow that? And there is evidence of that also with the United Nations. Did you know this? Or perhaps you didn't know that, but you said this?

utterances.speaker: YOUSSEF HAJIR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do you think if I had known that, I would have left my three daughters and my wife in Sarajevo? I would have contacted you, if possible, or anyone else in Republika Srpska, and I would have asked for anything just to get them out of there. I spent many sleepless nights because of them. And in spite of being tired and working hard, I had to be thinking about my family. And had I been able to get those folks of mine out, I would have done so to spare them the misery.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But this was a well-known fact. We were constantly appealing, through General Morillon and others, and it was constantly in the media. Mrs. Plavsic also was requesting freedom of movement, and we also signed, in Geneva and in London, several times the commitment to allow civilians to leave the zone of combat, and we respected that. But Mr. Izetbegovic said that he was not going to permit Sarajevo to empty itself. I'm sorry you didn't know that, but it is a fact. Here in paragraph 60 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do not make speeches. Dr. Hajir, do you agree?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, with what he said? Well, I said I didn't know what he was saying, I don't know if I agree or not. I was in the position that I was in. Thousands of people every day were passing by. I mean, I don't know. I don't agree with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In Article 60 -- I mean, in paragraph 60, you are thinking about what the objective of the Serbs was. If I were to tell you that the United Nations, and the witness confirmed that here, stated that the objective of the Serbs was to keep the 1st Corps in Sarajevo until a political solution was reached, does that then explain why the Serbs did not capture specific neighbourhoods, such as Dobrinja, or Sarajevo, itself?

utterances.speaker: YOUSSEF HAJIR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think that -- I mean, they took whatever -- I'm sorry. You are trying to approach and present this from your point of view, and that is your side. I am trying to talk about things as an individual, about things that I took part in and where I tried to help. So I really cannot agree that that was so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I am sorry about your heart attack, from Article 61, but do you agree that in these more recent statements of yours, in a way, the number of victims has grown, the number of operations, the number of wounded? How did it happen that in later statements, and Article 164 - this is more recent information dating from February of this year - there is a kind of inflation of the number of victims? The number of victims, the figures are bigger.

utterances.speaker: YOUSSEF HAJIR [Resumed]
utterances.text: The war was at its most intense in 1993 and 1994, so even in the summer of 1992, the numbers were not lower, either. But a higher intensity of the war was then, so it's logical to expect a greater number of victims as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think the witness has misunderstood the question. But nothing has been inflated. This has all been taken from prior testimony and/or prior statements of Dr. Hajir, the information contained in the amalgamated witness statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What paragraph was it?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, Dr. Karadzic -- Mr. Karadzic is just saying, generally, how come the figures are inflated now in the amalgamated statement, taken in February 2010, as opposed to prior statements and prior testimony. What I'm saying is there's no inflation in this statement; all of the figures come from either prior testimony or prior statements provided by the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic referred to Article 164, which I couldn't follow. What is it, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Generally speaking, this article gave me some kind of cue, it prompted me, because this statement, new information provided on the 25th of February, 2010, and then I remembered that there were 35 and 55 wounded, 35 soldiers and 55 civilians, and that there were 6 killed and 5 civilians killed in the football-match. Later, it appears that there were 140 wounded and 14 killed, so I was just interested how this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... what we dealt with minutes ago, when you clarified, Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, none of the new information provided by the witness on the 25th of February relates to figures of people killed or wounded during the war. What Mr. Karadzic keeps repeating about these 35 wounded or 55 wounded is a document that was put to Dr. Hajir by the Defence counsel in the Galic case, and it was a document, I think, that was actually signed by one of the military commanders. But it wasn't anything that Dr. Hajir has ever said. And his answer -- the question, a large portion of the document was read out, and then the question was: "Sir, you told us that Ismet Hadzic, after that event, would come to the hospital?" To which the witness replied: "Yes." That's what he was replying yes to was the question that the commander came to the hospital, not in relation to the number of dead and wounded, because he said earlier in the transcript in Galic -- at page 1708, it was put to him that roughly 140 people were admitted and there were 13 or 14 people killed: "Did you note --" The question was: "Did you note --" this is in cross-examination -- "for these people, whether these were soldiers or civilians? "A. To be quite honest, we never took note of whether a patient was a military man, a civilian, or anything else. We didn't take note of that."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Sutherland. Mr. Karadzic, I think it's time for you to wrap up your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I can have a little bit more time, just a few more questions which could be answered with a yes or a no. It would really be a pity not to complete this cross-examination. There is a large number of statements. Many have now been relativised, so I must ask the doctor if he knew about some crucial events.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I didn't understand that. I think you can conclude in 10 minutes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will try, and I'm going to ask Dr. Hajir that we proceed with Yes or No whenever possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you know that Mr. Izetbegovic declared a general mobilisation on the 4th of April, 1992?

utterances.speaker: YOUSSEF HAJIR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot remember the date, but he did declare a general mobilisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you know that Hasanefendic in April, on the 12th of April and the 29th of April, on two occasions, thus ordered attacks on the JNA, and the blocking of all barracks, and the barricading of all roads?

utterances.speaker: YOUSSEF HAJIR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know, do you recall that on the 2nd of May, near the Skenderija Bridge, several soldiers were killed, their cars were burned? They were on their way to evacuate soldiers from the JNA hall.

utterances.speaker: YOUSSEF HAJIR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw that in the news, but I wasn't nearby.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you recall that on the 3rd of May in Dobrovoljacka Street, there was a large massacre where half the JNA column -- of a half a JNA column that was withdrawing?

utterances.speaker: YOUSSEF HAJIR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard that there was an incident. I didn't hear of any massacre. I wasn't there, so I didn't see it, I didn't -- I wasn't there, so I really cannot give you any opinion on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you know that Alija Delimustafic, the minister of internal affairs, already on the 4th or 5th of May, accused Avdo Hebib, Ganic, Kljujic, and others of declaring war against the JNA and initiating a war against the JNA?

utterances.speaker: YOUSSEF HAJIR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't really know. I didn't know about that, no.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I now look at 1D13 -- I'm sorry, first we will look at 1092.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you know about the abuses of ambulance vehicles, that the army used ambulances in order to transport soldiers to positions, and so on and so forth?

utterances.speaker: YOUSSEF HAJIR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't approve of that, and I never had any part in such things. I don't even know if this happened. Our ambulances from Dobrinja were never abused. They were always marked. They were always shot at. There are big holes, small holes on the cars. Those vehicles were marked. Never, ever did we ever abuse that. I don't know about other such cases with ambulances.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I completely believe you, but this official note states that in your neighbourhood, close to you in Ilidza, the Green Berets, already on the 4th of May, 1992, abused vehicles marked as ambulances with the red cross. They used them for combat purposes. Do you see this official note?

utterances.speaker: YOUSSEF HAJIR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which one is it? Is it this one?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: There's a Serbian and an English version.

utterances.speaker: YOUSSEF HAJIR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you agree that this could have made the transport of your wounded to Sarajevo even more difficult, for which in the beginning you easily made agreements with Serbian check-points? Later, this was more difficult. Could such incidents have contributed to this distrust?

utterances.speaker: YOUSSEF HAJIR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course they could have, but they could have also inspected the cars, looked at the situation, and allowed the people through, pursuant to the agreement. This co-operation was severed, to the detriment of all of us, Serbs, Muslim, Croats, because those people could have received better treatment, better care, in a more -- in a better-equipped institution. So this was to the detriment of all of us. There is the Geneva Conventions. They condemned such things, misuses of medical vehicles and firing at such medical vehicles. However, these medical -- these Geneva Conventions were not respected, neither from your side and, I believe in certain cases, on the Muslim side too. Unfortunately, things are like that. May I comment, Mr. Karadzic? You have give some -- been given some space. May I also get some moments to give you my impressions about all of that?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, I would rather for us to meet when I return. Impressions don't help us much. We need information and knowledge here. I think that this would be nice. Unfortunately, we don't have enough time. Is it correct that your 30 to 40 employees, the hospital staff, were members of the B and H Army?

utterances.speaker: YOUSSEF HAJIR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. There were 43, and that's why this misunderstanding occurred. There were 43 members of the armed forces who were perhaps given an assignment, but they didn't go anywhere. They continued working in the hospital. But at one point, there were 158 staff. The number fluctuated all the time. Some people came, some people went away. People came from town to help out. Muslims and Serbs left the hospital on their own errands. The number varied all the time. We received everyone, however. And I don't see why something offered by the army would be refused. In that general poverty and misery, if anything can be received, then let it. But I wanted to register the hospital officially so that people get at least an allowance from the Ministry of Health.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you have a course of military surgery for your staff members?

utterances.speaker: YOUSSEF HAJIR [Resumed]
utterances.text: You see, in Dobrinja, Kuzmanovic and many other Serbs, very nice young men with whom I worked and met socially, Dr. Vranic organised, when the war in Croatia began, a course of military surgery, and at the beginning we were laughing. Nobody believed we'd ever need it. Interpersonal relations were still good among all ethnic communities. But in my hospital, I had to start from scratch because 90 per cent of staff were absent. First of all, I had to get hold of basic equipment. The first surgery I did with Dr. Vranic lasted seven hours. Transport was a problem. Blood transfusions were a problem. I had to send my staff to the Institute for Transfusions to teach them the basics. We had a crash course in emergency surgery. All sorts of things needed to be done preliminarily before the hospital took off.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this page be admitted, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Dr. Hajir, the document which is in front of you, called a memo, says that the Green Berets were in possession of two vans with Red Cross insignia on them. Did you know or hear such facts?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Never. I neither approve, nor have I ever heard of anything like that. You see, there's one thing with Mr. Karadzic. He ascribes and blames everything on Green Berets. There are --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Doctor, you said, did you not, that this could have contributed to distrust? Did you say that on a hypothetical basis?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What do you mean; those vehicles?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. And in answering the question by the accused, Dr. Karadzic, you confirmed that it might have contributed to distrust, so I was wondering whether you confirm that such abuses of ambulances really took place.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I did not confirm that, Judge. I'm just speaking, in very general terms, about using humanitarian vehicles for war purposes. I know nothing about this specific incident.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, we don't see a basis to admit this document. And I think it's time to conclude --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: -- your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I ask one more question? Can we see 1D135.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Dr. Hajir, you considered yourself, after November 1994, no longer a member of the BH Army, that is, the 155th Brigade?

utterances.speaker: YOUSSEF HAJIR [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But if you look at this document, they continue to consider you, as of the 9th of June, 1995, a member of the brigade. And in this report, concerning Operation Vranduk, involving the detachment called El Mujahid, information is provided to the General Staff of the BH Army about foreign nationals in Sarajevo, and it says: "Hasan Nemar, member of the 101st Brigade, Mustafa Bakou, member of the 101 Brigade, Khachouf, Habib, member of the 152nd Brigade, and Youssef Hajir, member of the 155th Brigade." They don't say anything unkind about you, but they have nothing good to say about the others. Do you know any of the people on that list?

utterances.speaker: YOUSSEF HAJIR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I still know Hasan and Mustafa, the first two on this list. The first one is an agronomy engineer who used the plot of land between Alipasino Polje and Cengic Vila. You know, there's a mosque there now and a disco. That area used to be empty, and he used it as a vegetable garden to feed people. I know Mr. Bakou now, but I didn't know him during the war. I didn't even know such a man existed. As for Mr. Khachouf, I don't know him at all. Now, that they considered me a member of the 155th Brigade in 1995, that's certainly a mistake. If I had been, I would be receiving a larger pension. The truth is that I was not a member at that time. If I had been, perhaps it would have been better for me, my pension would be higher.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we see the next page to see the signature and the reason why the El Mujahid Detachment got angry with the BH Army. If we could zoom in on the last-but-one paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It says: "The attitude of the El Mujahid Detachment towards the BH Army is characterised by a general lack of trust, which dates back to the events in autumn, 1992, when, in the course of capturing Cekrcici village, they were wedged because the BH Army did not secure their flanks." Do you know where Cekrcici is?

utterances.speaker: YOUSSEF HAJIR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I passed by several times. I really don't know anyone from the El Mujahid Detachment. I heard of their existence, but I really don't know these people. I don't know what they did and how they worked. I have no clue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me thank you, Dr. Hajir, for all that you've done as a doctor for Serbs, Muslims, and Croats alike, and for your testimony as well. May this document be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll mark it for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As MFI D857, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Without having to have a break -- yes, Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I'm sorry. The Prosecution does have a translation of that that we can send to the Defence to up-load into e-court. And I just note that in Dr. Karadzic's question, he said: "They don't say anything unkind about you, but they have nothing good to say about the others." In fact, after the four individuals are named, the sentence says: "We reported on them already in our documents. The persons in question lived in the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina before the aggression. We do not have at our disposal information on these persons that is of interest, in terms of intelligence." I think Dr. Karadzic was overstating what was, in fact, in the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I take it there's no objection to admitting that. We'll just admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I -- may I just explain? When I said, About you, They don't say anything about you, unkind about you, I meant the four of them. But the other members of the El Mujahid --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It's not necessary. Ms. Sutherland, do you have re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour. I was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I asked whether you --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, I don't. I'm sorry, I was discussing something with Mr. Reid, and I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Dr. Hajir, that concludes your evidence. Thank you very much for your taking time to give your testimony again to the Tribunal, and now you are free to go.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Well, unless there's other matters to raise, that will be it for today, and we will resume tomorrow at 2.15. The hearing is now adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 3rd day of November, 2010, at 2.15 p.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 10.34 a.m.,
